args.text:
If you're a program manager or a federal web developer, chances are someone's handed you what looks like a dead simple job: knock up a website for some initiative at your agency. Thing is, the real hard yakka usually isn't writing the content or designing the site. It's getting the security and privacy compliance sorted so you can actually launch the thing and keep it running. For that bit, you might have to bring in a contractor or pile even more onto your agency's already flat-out web team.

It shouldn't be like that.

## Why Pages?

Pages looks after our fellow federal partners by handling the backend and compliance work for launching and running a website, and doing it properly, so you can put your know-how into your content instead.

- **FedRAMP Certified Platform** Pages runs on cloud.gov, a platform whose security and compliance have been checked off by the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board, so you can count on your site being fast, reliable, and ready for whatever traffic rush comes out of nowhere.

- **Easy previews and content approvals** Pages builds draft updates to your site at a special preview URL. That way your team knows their changes will come out right when they're pushed to the main site, and it's easy to get the tick from the higher-ups on content updates.

[![Diagram of Pages architecture]({{site.baseurl}}/assets/images/pages/how-pages-works-diagram.png)]({{site.baseurl}}/assets/documents/how-pages-works-diagram.pdf)

## Why static websites?

Pages builds static websites instead of running a more complicated content management system (CMS) like Drupal or WordPress. Static sites have a few things going for them:

- **Less complexity and vulnerability:** Steering clear of a traditional CMS means steering clear of headaches like babysitting server applications (no PHP or Apache / IIS), plus all the database scaling and backup carry-on. A production-grade static site usually needs one simple static file server or service, not dozens of the things. So the whole site's easier to look after and has fewer holes in it.

- **Update content without writing code:** Static websites often keep their content in plain text files that anyone on the team can have a go at. The GitHub editor lets any team member do basic edits to their text files, whether they've written a line of code in their life or not.

- **Easy to host and maintain:** Hosting static website files on Pages is a piece of piss. Er, a piece of cake. You can make the most of scaling services like Amazon S3 through Pages, and you only pay for what you use.

- **Fully customizable:** Designers and developers can shape a static website into whatever they like without having to rip out the features and defaults a CMS lumps you with. You can build all sorts of sites with them, from organisation homepages or intranets to pre-generated web application program interfaces that show data from a separate server.
